module_title: Valuation and Analysis of Bonds with Embedded Options

payload.text: Under the arbitrage-free framework, the value of a bond with embedded options is the sum of the arbitrage-free values of its parts. Two equations follow from that, and almost everything else in the module is their consequence.
Callable bonds
The decision to exercise a call belongs to the issuer. The investor is therefore long the bond but short the call, so the option reduces the value of the callable bond relative to the straight bond.

payload.expr: Value of callable bond = Value of straight bond − Value of issuer call option
Value of issuer call option = Value of straight bond − Value of callable bond

payload.text: Putable bonds
The decision to exercise a put belongs to the investor, who is long both the bond and the option. The option therefore increases the value of the putable bond.

payload.expr: Value of putable bond = Value of straight bond + Value of investor put option
Value of investor put option = Value of putable bond − Value of straight bond

paras: The straight bond is easy — discount its cash flows at the appropriate spot rates. The hard part is valuing the option, because its value is contingent on future interest rates: the issuer's decision to call depends on the ability to refinance more cheaply. In practice the option value is often backed out as the difference between the straight and the callable bond, rather than valued directly.

Get the signs right and half this module is secure. Callable subtracts because the investor is short the option. Putable adds because the investor is long it. The party holding the option is the one who benefits from it.

payload.text: Valuing the default-free, option-free bond

Each cash flow is discounted at the spot rate corresponding to its payment date. Spot rates are not always directly observable but can be inferred from market prices of actively traded on-the-run sovereign bonds. Par rates, spot rates and forward rates are equivalent ways of conveying the same information — knowing any one determines the others.

units.title: How Interest Rate Volatility Affects Value

payload.text: One relationship governs this whole section, and it holds for both option types.

paras: The value of any embedded option, regardless of type, increases with interest rate volatility. Greater volatility means more opportunities for the option to be exercised.

payload.text: Volatility is represented through the dispersion of the interest rate tree. From each node rates may go up or down; the dispersion between those states is determined by the process generating rates from the yield curve and the volatility assumption. Higher volatility, wider dispersion.
The consequence differs by option type

rows: Falls — value of straight bond less a larger option
Rises — value of straight bond plus a larger option

payload.title: Volatility and the call option

blocks.text: A 30-year 4.50% bond callable at par in 10 years, on a 4% flat yield curve. The value of the straight bond is unaffected by volatility; only the option component moves.
Note that the straight bond value is the constant in this comparison. All movement in the callable bond comes from the option.

payload.answer: Option value more than triples; callable bond value falls accordingly

units.title: How the Yield Curve Affects Value

payload.text: Level and shape both matter, and they matter in opposite directions for calls and puts.
Level of the curve

rows: Moves into the money — issuer can refinance cheaply
Moves into the money — investor can reinvest higher

payload.text: The call caps the investor's upside. As rates fall, the straight bond appreciates freely but the callable bond does not, because no investor will pay more than the price at which the bond can be immediately called. The callable bond's value therefore rises less rapidly than the straight bond's, limiting upside potential.

paras: The put is a hedge against rising rates. As rates rise the straight bond declines, but the decline is partially offset by the increasing put value. On a move from a 3% flat curve to a 5% flat curve, the straight bond falls 30% while the putable bond's fall is limited to 22%.

payload.text: Shape of the curve
All else equal, the value of the call option increases as the yield curve flattens, and increases further if it inverts.
30-year 4.50% bond callable at par in 10 years, 15% interest rate volatility.

paras: The intuition: when the curve is upward sloping, one-period forward rates on the tree are high, so opportunities for the issuer to call are fewer. When the curve flattens or inverts, many nodes carry lower forward rates, which increases the opportunities to call.

payload.text: Moneyness at issue

items: Assuming a normal upward-sloping curve at issue, the call embedded in a callable bond issued at par is out of the money. It would not be called if the arbitrage-free forward rates at zero volatility prevailed.
Callable bonds issued at a large premium — common in the US municipal sector — are in the money, and will be called if the arbitrage-free forwards prevail.

units.title: Valuing a Callable Bond from the Tree

payload.text: The mechanics are backward induction from LM2 with one extra step at every node: check whether the option would be exercised.
The exercise rule

payload.expr: Callable: value at node = min(computed value, call price)
payload.label: Issuer exercises to its benefit

payload.expr: Putable: value at node = max(computed value, put price)
payload.label: Investor exercises to their benefit

payload.text: At each node, first compute the value by backward induction exactly as for a straight bond. Then apply the exercise rule. For a callable bond the issuer will call whenever the computed value exceeds the call price, so the node carries the lower of the two. For a putable bond the investor will put whenever the computed value falls below the put price, so the node carries the higher.

paras: The direction of the min/max is decided by who holds the option, not by which is bigger. The issuer holds the call and acts to reduce what it owes, hence min. The investor holds the put and acts to protect value, hence max.

payload.text: Backward induction with the exercise check

payload.expr: Value at node = [C + (0.5 × V<sub>H</sub> + 0.5 × V<sub>L</sub>)] / (1 + i)
payload.label: Compute first, then apply the exercise rule

payload.text: The value of the option itself is then recovered as the difference between the straight bond value and the callable value, which is generally easier than valuing the option directly.
For risky bonds, a spread must be added to the tree so the model reproduces the observed market price. Doing that in a way that strips out the option is what makes the spread comparable.

paras: The option-adjusted spread is the constant spread that, when added to all the one-period forward rates on the interest rate tree, makes the arbitrage-free value of the bond equal to its market price.

payload.text: Note the relationship to the Z-spread from LM1: the Z-spread for an option-free bond is simply its OAS at zero volatility. Once volatility is introduced, or an option is present, the two diverge.

blocks.text: A three-year 4.25% annual coupon bond callable at par in one and two years, at 10% interest rate volatility. Market price 101.000.
Trial 1 — add 30 bps to all forward rates

blocks.expr: Computed value = 100.973  →  below the market price of 101.000

blocks.text: The value is too low, meaning the discount rates are too high. Because price and yield move inversely, try a lower spread.

blocks.expr: Computed value = 101.010  →  slightly above the market price

blocks.text: The spread is added to the rates in the tree, not subtracted from the coupon. That distinction is directly examinable.

payload.text: How volatility affects OAS

paras: For a callable bond, holding the market price constant, an increase in the volatility assumption lowers the OAS.

payload.text: The mechanism: higher volatility raises the value of the call, which lowers the model value of the callable bond. To bring the model value back up to the unchanged market price, a smaller spread must be added to the tree. The option has absorbed more of the yield premium, leaving less to be attributed to credit and liquidity.

paras: This is why OAS matters for relative value. Two analysts using different volatility assumptions will compute different OAS for the same bond at the same price. An OAS comparison across bonds is only meaningful if the volatility assumption is consistent.

payload.text: Scenario analysis

Valuing bonds with embedded options over an investment horizon requires computationally intensive use of OAS technology, because the call or put decision must be evaluated against the evolution of interest rate scenarios during the holding period.

Performance over a horizon trades off reinvestment of cash flows against change in the bond's value. For a 4.5% bond with five years to maturity over a one-year horizon: if the bond is option free, higher rates increase reinvestment income but reduce terminal principal value. Because the horizon is short, reinvestment income is relatively insignificant and performance is dominated by the change in principal value — so lower rates give superior performance.
Yield duration measures assume cash flows do not change when yields change. That assumption is false for bonds with embedded options, which is why only one duration measure applies.
Why modified duration fails

rows: Benchmark interest rates — the government par curve
Expected cash flows do not change when yield changes
Cash flows may change with rates
Straight bonds and bonds with embedded options

payload.text: Because the values of embedded options are contingent on interest rates, the yield-duration assumption fails. For bonds with embedded options the only appropriate measure is effective duration, also called option-adjusted duration. Since it works for straight bonds too, practitioners tend to use it regardless of bond type.
It indicates sensitivity to a 100 bps parallel shift of the benchmark yield curve, specifically the government par curve.
Comparing the three bonds

paras: Neither a callable nor a putable bond can have effective duration exceeding that of the straight bond. Both options reduce duration relative to the option-free equivalent.

rows: Call out of the money; duration ≈ straight bond
Put out of the money; duration ≈ straight bond
Duration resembles a straight bond maturing on the first exercise date
Same — bond highly likely to be put on that date

payload.text: The mechanism in each case is the same. The call gives the issuer the right to retire the bond at the call price, which limits price appreciation when rates decline. The put limits price depreciation when rates rise, because the investor can put the bond and reinvest at a higher yield. Either way the option truncates one side of the price response, and a truncated response is a smaller duration.
Effective duration averages the up-shift and down-shift responses. When an option is near the money that average conceals more than it reveals.
The asymmetry problem

Effective durations are normally calculated by averaging the price changes from shifting the benchmark curve up and down by the same amount. That works for option-free bonds. With embedded options it misleads, because price sensitivity is not symmetrical to positive and negative rate changes of equal magnitude.

payload.title: Where the average breaks down

blocks.text: A 4.5% bond maturing in five years, immediately callable at 100, on a 4% flat yield curve at 15% volatility.
No matter how far rates decline, the price cannot exceed 100 — no investor pays more than the price at which the bond can be immediately called. The downside, by contrast, has no limit.
Averaging a capped up-move against an uncapped down-move produces a number that describes neither scenario.

payload.answer: Upside is capped at 100; downside is unbounded

paras:
One-sided durations — effective duration computed separately for rates up and rates down — capture this better than the two-sided measure, particularly when the embedded option is near the money.

For a callable bond, one-sided down-duration is much smaller than one-sided up-duration. For a putable bond the asymmetry runs the other way.

payload.text: Key rate duration

Effective duration measures sensitivity to a parallel shift. Key rate duration measures sensitivity to a change at a specific maturity segment, holding other segments constant, which allows shaping risk to be identified and managed.

This matters more for bonds with embedded options than for straight bonds, because the exercise decision depends on rates around the exercise date rather than on the curve as a whole. A shift concentrated near the call date affects a callable bond very differently from an equivalent shift at the long end.
Effective convexity

paras:
Callable bonds exhibit negative convexity when the call is near or in the money. The call truncates price appreciation, so the price–yield relationship bends the wrong way as rates fall.

Putable bonds always exhibit positive convexity. The put truncates price depreciation, which reinforces rather than opposes the natural curvature.

rows: Negative when rates are low and the call is in the money
Upside is capped at the call price
Positive throughout, and greater when the put is in the money
Downside is floored at the put price

paras: A question describing a bond whose price appreciates less than it depreciates for equal yield moves is describing negative convexity, and therefore a callable bond with the call near or in the money. This is one of the most reliably tested points in the module.

payload.text: Ten points for a final pass

items: Callable subtracts the option, putable adds it — determined by which party holds the option.
Option value rises with volatility for both types; the effect on the bond is opposite.
The call caps upside as rates fall; the put floors downside as rates rise.
Call option value rises as the curve flattens or inverts, because more tree nodes carry low forwards.
At the node, callable takes the minimum and putable the maximum against the exercise price.
OAS is the constant spread added to the tree rates that reproduces the market price.
Z-spread equals OAS at zero volatility for an option-free bond.
Higher assumed volatility lowers the OAS of a callable bond at a given price.
Neither callable nor putable duration can exceed straight-bond duration.
Callable bonds go negatively convex near the money; putable bonds stay positively convex throughout.
